report:
## Yes—moderate evidence supports this claim

Olive leaf extract (OLE), rich in the polyphenol oleuropein, does appear to lower blood pressure, based on both human clinical trials and mechanistic research.

**Key evidence:**

The strongest human trial is a double-blind, randomized, active-controlled study of 232 patients with stage-1 hypertension comparing OLE (500 mg twice daily) to the ACE-inhibitor drug Captopril (12.5–25 mg twice daily) over 8 weeks. Both treatments produced statistically similar reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and OLE additionally improved triglyceride and LDL cholesterol levels (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/).

A summary review of an earlier double-blind study found that 1,000 mg/day of OLE produced significant reductions in blood pressure and cholesterol in people with stage-1 hypertension, with higher doses (1,000 mg vs. 500 mg) producing greater effects (https://naturalhealthresearch.org/olive-leaf-lowers-blood-pressure/).

Examine.com's evidence-based research summary corroborates this, noting OLE's phenolic compounds (especially oleuropein) are linked to blood-pressure reduction, improved lipid profiles, and reduced inflammation across multiple studies (https://examine.com/supplements/olive-leaf-extract/research/).

Mechanistically, oleuropein is thought to promote vasodilation and improve endothelial function, partly by increasing nitric oxide availability and reducing oxidative stress—plausible biological pathways supporting the clinical findings (https://www.chenlangbio.com/knowledge/what-makes-oleuropein-powder-a-best-seller-in-natural-extracts).

**Caveats:** The evidence base is still relatively small—mostly short-term trials (weeks, not years) with modest sample sizes, primarily in people with mild (stage-1) hypertension rather than severe cases. More large-scale, long-term RCTs are needed to confirm optimal dosing, durability of effects, and safety alongside conventional antihypertensive medications. Overall, current evidence reasonably supports "yes," with appropriate caution about strength and generalizability.
